Iran International, Oct 2026

Attacks on vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz have intensified, with at least 10 ships struck since Sunday, the highest number over the period since the US-Israel war with Iran began.

Iran's ongoing war has consequences for the entire world, comparable to those of a world war, IRGC General Yadollah Javani said on Wednesday.

The IRGC Navy said on Wednesday that a container ship carrying more than 2,500 containers sank in waters south of the Strait of Hormuz after striking a naval mine and catching fire.

Iran should seek an agreement to end the war with the United States, as former supreme leader Ruhollah Khomeini did during the Iran-Iraq war, former Tehran mayor Gholamhossein Karbaschi said in an interview with state television.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations has recorded 20 reported attacks in the Strait of Hormuz since Oct. 1, with vessels struck by “unknown projectiles,” including two incidents reported Wednesday.

No country is willing to sell Iran military equipment, a senior Iranian army official said, adding that Tehran has therefore had to rely on weapons developed domestically.

“As you know, no country sells us equipment that we can simply go and buy,” said Habibollah Sayyari, the coordinating deputy of Iran’s regular military.

Sayyari said the armed forces, Defense Ministry and universities were relying on Iranian engineers and researchers to develop new equipment, adding that the military would use those systems to respond to future threats.

100%Oct 15, 2026, 06:48 GMT+1Iran says IRGC intelligence arrested suspects over anti-establishment activityThe prosecutor in Kerman, in southeastern Iran, said the Revolutionary Guards’ intelligence arm arrested members of a group accused of setting fire to sites and coordinating anti-establishment activities.

Authorities described the detainees as linked to “counter-revolutionary” groups, a term commonly used by the Islamic Republic for its opponents, but did not identify any organization.

Iranian lawmaker Esmail Kowsari said on Thursday that an energy agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin would be difficult to implement and would not reduce the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz.

“The United States cannot make up for its energy shortage through this agreement or diminish the importance of the Strait of Hormuz,” said Kowsari, a member of parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee.

Prolonged war and renewed disruptions to energy production, shipping routes or critical infrastructure pose the biggest risk to economies across the Middle East and Central Asia, the International Monetary Fund said on Thursday.

The IMF expects the Middle East, North Africa and Pakistan region to contract 1.3% in 2026 after 3.3% growth last year, before rebounding 6.6% in 2027.

Jihad Azour, the IMF’s Middle East and Central Asia director, said pre-war surpluses, alternative trade routes and inventory drawdowns had limited the initial impact of disruptions caused by the war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, but warned those buffers were finite.

Failure by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan to move fertilizer through the Strait of Hormuz could trigger a food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, a senior UN official told Reuters.

UN Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva said the mechanism could be activated within seven to 10 days of an agreement, warning that further delays risk missing the planting season.

He said as few as five vessels a day could keep fertilizer supplies moving to countries in critical need. Fertilizer shipments from the Persian Gulf region have remained largely halted for more than six months.

The US military has developed new strike plans for Iran that include the possible use of its most powerful non-nuclear bomb against energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders renewed attacks, CNN reported on Thursday.

The plans include potential use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, known as the MOAB or “mother of all bombs,” CNN said, citing multiple US officials and people familiar with military planning.

One source told CNN that Trump had ordered additional strike packages covering “a lot of energy infrastructure” and potentially involving the MOAB. Another said plans for attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities, including the site known as Pickaxe Mountain, explicitly included the weapon.

No decision to carry out the strikes has been reported. A White House official told CNN that the administration does not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist, adding that Trump “keeps all options on the table” to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

Questions over effectiveness against underground sites

The 21,600-pound, or roughly 9.8-metric-ton, MOAB is designed to produce a powerful blast over a wide area rather than penetrate deeply buried targets.

Sources cited by CNN questioned whether the weapon could destroy Iranian nuclear facilities protected by rock deep underground. One person familiar with the planning described it as effective for clearing a large area but “definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead.”

The report said its large blast radius could also raise concerns about civilian casualties if used against infrastructure near populated areas.

The United States first used the MOAB in combat in Afghanistan in 2017, when it struck an Islamic State tunnel complex during Trump’s first presidency.

CNN reported that US military planners have also prepared other potential options as the administration considers how to bring the conflict with Iran to an end. Trump has said Iran will not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon and has indicated in recent days that further US action remains possible.

US President Donald Trump said Wednesday that Iran was asking in negotiations with Washington to be “allowed to live,” adding, “They don’t want us to go after them.”

“Now their main thing that they ask in negotiation is, ‘Will you please allow us to live?’” Trump said, speaking at a campaign rally in Kalispell, Montana.

Trump said Iran no longer had a navy or air force, described its army as “decimated” and said successive levels of its leadership had been killed, adding that he no longer knew “who the hell we’re negotiating with.”

“We’re going to knock this Iran thing off fast. It’s going to be over very quickly,” Trump said.

He said the conflict would end “one way or the other” and predicted oil prices would fall once it was over.

Oil prices fell more than $1 in early Asian trading Thursday as investors weighed risks to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz against US efforts to lower petroleum transportation costs, Reuters reported.

Brent crude futures fell 1.31% to $104.67 a barrel by 0116 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude dropped 1.07% to $94.07, reversing gains from the previous session.

WTI had risen to a three-week high Wednesday after Iran-backed Houthis attacked Saudi Aramco’s headquarters and Iran said it was deploying new tactics to target ships in the Strait of Hormuz and keep oil prices high.

Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said in a post on X that the coalition intercepted and destroyed a drone in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province Wednesday.

The Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Iran, Russia and Venezuela, in an effort to reduce record-high global freight rates, Reuters reported Wednesday, citing a US official.

The discussions center on potentially allowing non-sanctioned crude and petroleum products to be transported on previously sanctioned vessels. The official said the goal was to move more crude and refined products out of the Persian Gulf.

Companies seeking to use the vessels would have to apply to the US Treasury Department, the official said. The Energy Department said any sanctions relief for the shadow fleet would not allow Russia to move sanctioned oil or petroleum products.

Maritime industry sources told Reuters that easing US restrictions was unlikely to lead to a broad decline in freight rates because ship insurers would remain bound by European Union and British regulations.
